//fonts: Styles offered by the font picker. Five of them are `bundled`: that face ships with the app under fonts/, so the option is always offered and always looks the same everywhere — it is never probed for, and it could not be, since web fonts load after the probe runs. `families` are faces already on the device that would also do; they sit *behind* the bundled name in the stack, so they only ever render what the subset deliberately leaves out (kanji, mostly, in the write-mode input). An option with no `bundled` is device-only: it is probed at startup and hidden if none of its families are present or if it renders identically to an option already listed. Options with neither are the device's own generic faces.

//charts: Reference tables for the chart sheet, laid out like the standard gojūon charts. LAYOUT ONLY where possible: a grid cell is a kana string (null = gap in the grid) and a flow item is a kana string, and app.js looks the romaji up from the decks below so the two can never disagree. A flow item may instead be {q, a} to carry its own reading, for a character that is reference-only and in no deck — none ships now that the extended katakana are a deck of their own. `type` is "grid" (consonant rows × vowel columns), "flow" (a wrapping list) or "numbers" (rows of {n, x, q, a} — what the row is, how it is written, the kana, the reading). `x` is optional and holds kanji: 六, 二十日, 月曜日 — what the drill puts on the square — while `n` names the row in plain terms, 6 or Monday or the 20th. A "numbers" section carries all four itself, because there is no deck of numbers or of dates to look a reading up from; every entry in the two shipped ones was generated by readNumber() and kanjiNumber() rather than typed, which is how the charts and the drills are kept from disagreeing. `wide` gives it one item per row, for a form too long to sit beside another.

//derived: Decks with no cards of their own: app.js builds each at boot from the `sources` it names, holding those decks' own card objects rather than copies, so a card cannot be in a source deck and missing from here. `script` places it under a seal stamp exactly as it does for a real deck — "kana" is the third stamp, the one for material that is both scripts at once. Each source deck is also one *category* to the balanced deal that orders a run: the categories are shuffled independently and then dealt out so that no more than two consecutive cards come from the same one, which is why these cannot be replaced by concatenating the sources and shuffling. Whether write mode has to name a script is derived from `sources` spanning more than one, never declared here.

//numbers: The number drills, and the one section here that is not a list of cards — 1 to 1,000,000 cannot be enumerated, so app.js *composes* a reading out of these parts and the drills generate their prompts from it. `ones` are the digits 1–9 read alone; `alt` and `altk` are the other readings that are also right (四 is yon or shi, 七 nana or shichi, 九 kyuu or ku) — see below for which of the two is graded. `places` are 千 百 十 within a group of four digits, biggest first, each carrying the `forms` its own sound changes produce — 三百 is sanbyaku, 六百 roppyaku, 八千 hassen. `groups` are the multipliers above 9999. The difference between the two is the leading 一: a place drops it (10 is juu, never ichijuu) and a group keeps it (10,000 is ichiman, never man), which is the whole reason they are separate lists rather than one. Reaching 億 or 兆 is one more `groups` entry plus a wider band in NUM_BANDS; nothing else changes. A drill is `{id, kind, len, max, label, sample, subtitle}` — `kind` is "count" (1 to `max`, each value once) or "random" (`len` values dealt across the magnitude bands); `len` is how many prompts a run is. Which way round a prompt goes is the answer mode's to decide, never the drill's. `alt` is the romaji and `altk` the kana; Writing accepts either, so both are graded — see CLAUDE.md for why romaji is an answer here and never is for a deck. Note that neither is carried into a compound — 40 is yonjū and 400 yonhyaku, never shijū or shihyaku — so the drill teaches the counting forms rather than accepting everything that has ever been said. `operators` and `percent` are what the "math" drill reads a sum with: each operator is a word said between two composed numbers — 三たす四 is san tasu yon — with `sym` the sign Writing asks with and `min`/`max` the range its operands are drawn from; which pairs are allowed (a minus that stays positive, a divide that comes out whole) is arithmetic and lives in app.js. `percent` is said *after* its number and joined to the whole with の — 二百の二十五パーセント, 25% of 200 — and like a calendar counter it lists in `irregular` the values whose reading changes as a whole: 十 before パ is じゅっ (or じっ), so 10, 20 and 50 are written out. Only the `values` a drill can ask need listing, and none of them ends in 4, 7 or 9. A "math" drill names the kinds it deals in `ops` and deals them evenly across `len`; its answer is the result, and a card files under its operator, so the report can say you are slow on わる.

//calendar: The calendar and the clock. Days, months, hours and minutes are all counting with a counter on the end, so they are *composed* the same way a number is — app.js reads the value with readNumber(), writes it with kanjiNumber() and appends the counter — and only what composition gets wrong is written down. `irregular` is that list, keyed by the whole value rather than by a digit, because these replace the entire reading and not one part of it: 一日 is tsuitachi, 二十日 hatsuka, 四月 shigatsu. Everything absent from it is built, kanji included — nothing here writes a kanji form out, since `j` in `numbers` above already says how a value is written. The rule that decides what has to be listed is the trailing digit: 4, 7 and 9 carry `alt` readings in `numbers` (yon/shi, nana/shichi, kyū/ku), and a bare trailing digit takes them — so every value ending in one of the three is written out here, or the drill would quietly accept jūnananichi for 十七日. `suffix` is the counter's own kanji, which the composed form ends in. `weekdays` are not counting at all and are simply listed — `en` is the identity, the thing Typing and Choosing answer with, where a day or a month answers with its number. Their `altk`/`alt` is the stem alone, げつ for げつようび: every weekday ends in the same ようび, so Writing takes either the whole word or just the part that says which day. That works for weekdays and for nothing else here — a month's stem is the bare number and a date's is either the bare number or nothing separable at all, so accepting it would drop the counter the drill is about. A drill is {id, kind, len, label, sample, subtitle}, `kind` being "week" or a counter id; every value is asked exactly once. The clock adds two more counters and nothing else: 時 on an hour and 分 on a minute, listed the same way and irregular in the same places — 四時 is yoji and 一分 ippun, and 分 is ふん after 2, 5 and 7 and ぷん after the rest, which is why most of the minutes are written out. `half` is the one reading that is not a counter at all: 半 han is half past, true of 3:30 and not of a bare 三十分, so app.js merges it into the minute only when the two counters are being said together. A drill may carry `values` instead of `len` — the values it asks, a subset of the same material rather than a second kind of thing, which is what `cal-day-native` is: the thirteen dates that are said as words instead of ending in にち. The list is the length, so it carries no `len`, and Choosing draws its wrong answers from the list too — offering the 19th against はつか in a drill that never asks it would answer the question for anyone who knows which thirteen are in it. A drill of `kind` "time" is the one built from two counters rather than one: it names them in `counters` and the marks it asks in `minutes`, and every value it asks is an hour and a minute said one after the other — which is the only thing the clock adds to how a reading is put together. Which way round a prompt goes is the answer mode's to decide, exactly as it is for the number drills. `meridiem` is 午前 and 午後, each with the 24-hour `from` its half of the day starts at; a time drill with `"meridiem": true` says one before the hour, is answered on the 24-hour clock, and asks only the `hours` it lists — 1 to 11, because whether 午前12時 is noon or midnight depends on whom you ask.
